She sends a small sum of money. She urges courage, serenity and patience.

M.A.F.

My Superior,

  1. I hope that by now you have received my letter with 120 francs. My dear, I would have sent you more, but I am always afraid they will get lost.1 You cannot imagine how sorry I was to hear you were without money; I am most grieved, and certainly it will never happen again. If you want more I will send you more. Now I am sending you another 5 francs. You will say: they are notes. And how am I to manage so that you get them quickly?

  2. My health is bad, and I would have sent for the doctor if Papa had not come to see me. I have lost my voice, I feel I am suffocating, I cough and have a malaise I cannot describe. We have had a great deal of work for head and body, as we had to send away all Teresa's2 belongings. I have received many daughters. The bursar is still here and works very hard. With two who are to come tomorrow, we are 19. My dear, now everything is being settled and I hope to come and embrace you soon, unless they bleed me.

  3. Today I am writing to everyone; give Rosa this one, which came from Genoa. I wrote to the Manager,3 replying to his letter, which I had the pleasure of receiving.

  4. Courage, my dear, the Lord wants to be glorified in adversity; so do not be distressed, be of good heart; the Lord loves you very much, believe it! Yes, Jesus caresses you; you, my good Superior, are always in my thoughts; yesterday's letter consoled me greatly, and I assure you, dear, that apart from your distress the rest consoled me,4 and I assure you that so far they are the only consolations I have. Carry on and

pray; do not forget the Fridays. Mind, exactness in everything.

5. Greet Fr. Paolo for me and write to me something about the Pieve.5 Goodbye, receive the blessing of your most loving mother, and I am

your Mother Rosa

6. At this moment I have received another letter from you. Patience, dear, and receive a thousand blessings from her who implores them from Heaven, and believe that I am and always will be your Mother. Still unwell. This evening I will send for the doctor as soon as Papa has left.

1 The Sisters had not yet received any payment. Hence the Mother's concern that they should not lack money for their daily needs.

2 Teresa Porta, widow Morasso. A friend of Mother Rosa and one of the first five companions. She did not take the habit of the Daughters of Saint Anne and left the Institute for good in April 1867. Cf. Arch St FSA, letter of Teresa Morasso of 21.4.1867, Pos Amiche.

3 The Manager, Marquis Giuseppe Rusconi. Under the Statute the Manager held a role of the first importance. To him was entrusted «the administration: he presides over discipline; supervises the medical and religious services; checks that the food is of good quality; decides on improvements, including those of a hygienic and sanitary nature...». Cf. work cited, Letter 7, n. 2.

4 She refers to the letters the other sisters had written to her.

5 Cf. Letter 11, n. 5.

She confides that she is «in the most terrible anguish» and asks for prayers. She assures her, however, that she finds «relish» in suffering.

M.A.F.

God bless you, dear Superior,

  1. It was with the greatest pleasure that I received your dear letter, which, I assure you, I was longing for.

  2. My dear, I am in the most terrible anguish. Pray and have others pray, that I may always keep peace and cheerfulness under the weight of so heavy a cross. I assure you that I am content and that it always seems little to me; but I know too that if he who gives me this relish in suffering1 withdrew even a little, ah! I would certainly be the ugliest monster and everything in me would be lost. Ah, good Jesus! From thorns, my Superior, he draws a balmy ether to intoxicate us. I am sure you too will ask him for this and that beloved Jesus will grant it to you.2 As for what you tell me about Teresa, stand firm, for the love of God; do not allow her to go to anyone other than the one you all go to. Firm, for charity's sake; do not let yourself be won over by arguments or anything else.3

  3. I enclose a five-franc note, and then, if it arrives safely, I will send you more at once. I thought it best not to put them in the basket I am sending you, as it does not seem safe enough. Write to me every day if you can, for I want you to.4

  4. Greet all the Daughters for me and give them my blessing, and believe me always

your Mother, who loves you in Jesus

1 Relish in suffering. As food nourishes and satisfies the body and makes it grow, so suffering (sharing in Christ's paschal mystery) nourishes and satisfies the soul. Such relish is a gift of Jesus. He draws a balmy ether from thorns. The Mother's language, typical of the mystics, reveals her experiential knowledge of living Christ, the Crucified, her Good.

2 Such a gift is not the exclusive privilege of a few. Let them ask for it and beloved Jesus will grant it.

3 This evidently concerns an additional service that Teresa Merlano offered to perform.

4 Besides strengthening unity and communion, frequent correspondence was necessary to keep her informed about daily life and events, which were full of unpleasant conflicts.

Various news: of her own poor health, of the cholera, of a consignment of food.

A.M.F.1

Dear Superior, beloved of Jesus,

  1. Just two lines, gathering all my strength to show you that today I am up, but only just. May the will of our dear Jesus be done.

  2. Yesterday I received your dear letters. I assure you they were a real consolation to me and made me laugh; I needed it, and especially yours, dear Superior. God bless you; bear everything patiently, for I will come as soon as I can.

  3. Here the cholera is still raging, as it is in Milan, and I must go and fetch my Carlottina, because the director has written to say so. It must be so as not to bear the responsibility.2

  4. Yesterday, as soon as I received your letter, I sent you by the 12 o'clock service a sack of potatoes3 and a basket of pears. I want you to eat this fruit yourselves, without giving it away. I hope you will.

  5. As soon as I can I will send you the veils and something else; for charity's sake, do not fast to save money; eat; spend what you like, eat well as your state requires.4 If you have no money, write and tell me, and I will send it at once. No, dear, I never meant to scold you about expenses! Poor thing! Believe me, I see everything and I am very pleased with your excessive thrift.

  6. Go on keeping the girls cheerful.5

  7. Dear Daughters of Saint Anne, love, love Jesus and become victims of charity;6 I envy you. I am idle, almost always lying down, with a weakness that is killing me, but happier than ever to do what God wills.

8. You say nothing about the Manager; did you greet him? Tell him to write to us, for I am impatiently awaiting a letter from him. I have had nothing yet from the Canon.7 Give my warmest greetings to the doctor's wife, her husband and Graziella, to everyone, to the Bursar.8 I can write no more. I close, and as long as I live I am

Your loving Mother [...]

1 From this letter onwards the initials M.A.F. become A.M.F., giving greater prominence to the figure of Saint Anne in the Institute named after her. 2 This brief mention shows the Mother's attention to the problem; among other things, it obliges her to provide directly and personally for her thirteen-year-old daughter by taking her in with her in Piacenza. In 1864 Carlotta was at the Royal Institute for the Deaf and Dumb in Milan, directed by Fr. Eliseo Ghislandi. Cf. Index II, 18.

3 Pomi di terra = potatoes.

4 Motherly solicitude and watchful attention to everything that could foster the physical and spiritual health of the sisters, all very young, engaged in the heavy general services (kitchen, linen room) of the hospital and in nursing the sick, and so exposed also to the danger of infection.

5 The girls, that is, the sisters. A very important recommendation. Joy and serenity are needed in order to grow in the spiritual life and devote oneself to the service of charity. But in difficult situations attention must be redoubled, so that zeal is not broken by sadness; Mother Rosa wanted sadness wholly banished from her daughters' hearts and never tired of urging them to be cheerful.

6 The expression signifies the soul and style of the Daughters of Saint Anne's «service» to the sick.

7 Fr. Michele Vaccari, confessor of the religious community. Cf. letter of Francesca Camisa, 11.7.1867.

8 Her cordial relations with the lay staff reveal Mother Rosa's human richness and her gift for relationships. The doctor is the head physician, Dr Didaco Facchini; his wife, Signora Irene Fortini; Graziella, their daughter; the bursar, Carlo Leonesi.

Accepting suffering and bearing everything cheerfully for love of Jesus. How to deal with the hospital bursar.

A.M.F. My Superior,

  1. Your letter was no great consolation to me, hearing that you are still so tormented by sadness; my dear, how can you hope to have consolation and peace as long as we dwell in this tearful vale of weeping? You know what lies in suffering, don't you? Yes, I seem to hear you answer me. Jesus, the beloved of your heart, the very being of your every thought, isn't that so? Well then, my dear, everything we do, everything is for Jesus. Dear Superior, rest assured that he accepts your sufferings, and in time you will feel the effects of this suffering of yours.1

  2. You ask me what you should do in the evening. I answer that you know well that this is the house of patience and sacrifice; well then, the rosary: if you cannot say it with the others, say it alone, showing your daughters your sorrow, but also that for Jesus everything must be borne cheerfully, even depriving ourselves of what is dearest to us; but always for Jesus; so our dear mamma Saint Anne teaches us.2

  3. Now, my dear, let us come to temporal matters. It would be good to get an advance from the bursar each time on the hospital expenses, because, I tell you, did you see what happened with Bernardi, from whom, as I see, we shall get nothing more?3 And yet it was a good sum. He and the others, who were cunning, used to do it. However, now I am sending you ten francs. If you think it right to mention it, do so; if not, I will see to it; or else I had thought that you might tell the bursar that I would send him a case of fine pears for the sick, and lint, if he wishes; I wanted to write to him, but you know well that they are always men and it is not fitting; it is

better that you let him know. But I do not want you to put yourself out at all. These are things you will do if you like; if not, leave it all, because, as you know, they buy them in Bologna, so dark and coarse; surely, it seems to me, they will be more welcome without any expense; what do you say?

  1. My dear, if I make these remarks about money, it is because, to tell you in confidence, and let no one know, we have had so many expenses, and I assure you that I am in a very bad way in this respect; but I hope in the Lord's mercy, that he will help us; it greatly distresses me, not because I lack trust, but you know well how many things there are.4

  2. Do not speak of what I am writing to you, and do not write me anything about it by way of condolence. Only what you have done with the Bursar.5

  3. As for your clothing, you cannot have it for now, because I wish to make the Exercises, since I am here. When I return to Cento, come here for the feast of Saint Francis. That is what we have arranged with your Father Tornatore.6 Write to him a little; put a couple of lines in one of my letters; have all your Daughters sign, calling him father and, if you think fit, first Father. Do not answer me anything about this either, for I am always afraid. Do it without saying anything to me. Goodbye, dear Superior.

God bless us, and may Saint Anne give us courage to bear everything with patience.

I am your most loving Mother Rosa

1 The tone is confidential, the style that of a dialogue, the content centred on the core of the Mother's spiritual teaching: love of the Cross. «You know what lies in suffering, don't you?» An expression that gives lift, resolve and courage more than a long speech.

2 Over time the figure of Saint Anne takes on affective and spiritual colouring.

3 There was little transparency and some illicit profit at the sisters' expense. Bonaventura Bernardi was the Superior General of the «Concettini» (cf. Letter 10, n. 3). Since one of the conditions for engaging the Sisters was that they should «appear as a single institution together with the Hospitaller Brothers», he had collected, along with the pay due to his religious, two hundred francs intended for the Sisters, but had not yet handed them over to the Superior.

4 She does not hide her own financial straits. She had taken in the cholera orphans at the Mother House.

5 Caution in writing. Letters were tampered with and checked; hence the Mother's fears, which were certainly not unfounded.

6 Fr. Tornatore's influence was growing. He was already regarded as the spiritual

father of the community; first Father, certainly in relation to Fr. Luigi Cogrossi, Director of the Work. The young women who made up the community, including the superior, had not yet received the religious habit, for two reasons: the climate in the hospital was unfavourable to religious, so that the Concettini had presented themselves as a lay association in civilian dress; and the Institute, moreover, was only just beginning. Nor did the Church yet have a canonical procedure with precise norms for Institutes of active life; these were in fact approved by the Sacred Congregation of Bishops and Regulars with the document «Secundum quas» in 1901. The Rule of the Institute provided for two months of postulancy before clothing and three years of probation, after which profession of temporary religious vows was made. Arch St FSA B. 1. 61.

The comforting news about how things are going at the hospital is a reason to thank God and Mother Saint Anne. Enlightening advice on the virtuous life, and recommendations.

A.M.F.

Dear Superior,

  1. Your comforting news was a true consolation to me, and I had it in still more detail from the Marquis, the Manager, who was kind enough to inform me of everything; let us thank God and our dear Saint Anne, and may these good protectors, that is, workers of his Work.1

  2. Now let us come to the cook. Tell her that to be admitted to the clothing, that is, to make simple vows, she must practise true obedience to the Superior, and that this does not consist in eating the virtue of a good soup but in abandoning herself to the will of her Superior. The probation is made for this, and not to see whether they do penances or eat little; no, because on the contrary, tell her, I see in that a great deal of caprice and not true virtue, and it shows that she needs more experience, because if by [chance] she went on doing things her own way and fell ill, we would have to think again; and besides, her constitution needs everything to keep her on her feet. So let her try to get certain notions out of her head, which can only be diabolical suggestions.2

  3. Tell the others that I am busy writing the prayer but have no time. As for you, dear, I tell you to take great care of yourself and turn to God often during the day, for then you will be calmer about your communion; and the doubt that I might take it from you is nothing but a temptation of the enemy to distress you;3 but be

sure that I have not the slightest thought of it. Only that of confirming you further; but, for charity's sake, always be on your guard, so that the wolves, alas close by, may not bite you;4 I pray for this every day. God grant that my prayers be heard.

  1. Today I am sending you the maize flour with a few other little things and a small box, which you will send discreetly to the Manager.

  2. Tell my dear girls to keep humble, the only way not to fall and to become saints; and tell them too that I want to see something in their own hand.

What is Eufemia doing? For charity's sake, tell her not to linger in the linen room and not to go there alone. Tell Rosa to be cheerful in moderation; the others are to be composed when they go to the laundry and not laugh too much, especially when there are men about.5

6. I must close, for I have no time. Receive the blessing of one who so unworthily bears the name of mother, and believe me

your most loving mother Rosa

1 For the moment, then, the difficulties within the hospital had been smoothed over.

2 With severity and firmness the Mother cuts short mistaken ideas about true virtue. Holiness does not consist in arbitrary fasting but in obedience. The superior is to help the young woman discern where her penitential choices come from.

3 An allusion to a custom later codified (cf. Fr. Tornatore, Applicazioni Regole comuni delle Delegate, ch. 4, 28): every Sunday the superior renewed the sisters' «permission» to receive Eucharistic communion daily during the following week.

4 Advice of extreme prudence. Events had clearly shown the Mother the motives fuelling hostility towards the sisters.

5 Advice to the postulants. The Mother knows them, wants direct correspondence with them too, and likes to say the needed word and give the right suggestion. The young women she mentions are Eufemia Mirasole and Rosa Podestà.

She will answer the postulants as soon as possible. They are to write to her directly and hand the Superior the letter sealed. «The month» of Saint Anne is to be kept.

A.M.F.

Dear Superior,

  1. Just two lines to answer your dear letter. For now I cannot answer my dear girls, but I will as soon as I can; indeed I am busy composing a little prayer.1

  2. Then I would like Daria and the others, when they write to me, to write separately and hand the letter to you sealed, so that they can tell me what is in their hearts more openly.2

  3. I also want you to keep the month of Saint Anne, which you will certainly have begun.3 Pray, dear Superior: prayer is the only weapon to defend ourselves against so many insidious dangers.

  4. Write to me at once. I recommend humility and the observance of the Rules to you. Today we have exposition.4 Fr. Luigi still in Rome.5

Greet everyone for me, the doctor's wife6 and everyone. Goodbye,

I am your most loving Mother Rosa

1 The postulants had asked the Mother to write a prayer for them.

2 Until then they had handed their letters to the Superior. The Mother respects the right to secrecy of conscience in the sisters' dealings with her.

3 A daily para-liturgical celebration throughout July, during which texts written by Fr. Tornatore were read to deepen knowledge of the holy Mother of Mary Immaculate. He himself had composed the booklet, which he gave to Mother Rosa with an accompanying letter on 27 March 1866.

4 Eucharistic adoration at the Mother House was frequent.

5 Fr. Luigi Cogrossi.

6 The wife of the hospital's head physician, Signora Irene Fortini Facchini. M. Rosa corresponded with her; cf. Arch St FSA, Posiz. Cento.

She describes Carlotta's first communion celebration in Milan. She instructs all the Sisters on the theological life in the charitable service of the sick and in community life.

A.M.F.

Dear Superior,

  1. Just two lines, because I am so busy that I cannot stay long with you, and still more because of my poor health, which always makes me fail in every duty. Today I suffered a great deal, because I went to visit a sick woman who lived very far away, so I leave you to imagine what such a long outing did to me.

  2. I went to Milan on the 4th of this month to see Carlottina make her communion.1 I left Piacenza at three in the morning and reached Milan at ten to five. There I went to a church to receive Communion, and at half past six I went to the school. Dear Superior, what can I say: it pleased the Lord that when I came out of the school I was seized by such a violent headache that, as soon as I reached my sister-in-law's house, while everyone was at the communion ceremony, I had to go to bed, suffering horribly. At twelve my mother2 went to fetch the girl and brought her to me. But no! I got up, but was soon lying down again, practically on a sofa, and dear Carlottina insisted on staying beside me the whole time until five, when the pain eased somewhat. We went to table, and afterwards my sister-in-law took the girl back to the school, and my mother, Caterina3 and I returned to Piacenza, arriving at 11 at night. They fumigated us; my dear, we thought we would die; Caterina, with the breathlessness she suffers from, was choked by such a stench. It was enough to kill you.

  3. Now settled in Piacenza, but there is a world of things to sort out and then, as you know, the Exercises.4 I thought it best that you should come for the feast of Saint Francis.5

  4. I was sorry to keep hearing the story about the broth, but you must not mind it, since the Bursar tastes it every day; enough: to live securely and in peace, ask the Bursar from time to time whether it is all right, and pay no attention to the rest.

  5. Tell the girls that I always mean to send them a little keepsake, but I have no time and do not know how to manage it.

  6. Fr. Luigi6 has not come yet; here we enjoy a paradise of peace, everything goes with perfect exactness; I hope it is the same there.

  7. They will love one another with one heart and always mirror themselves in their Spouse Jesus, to see in him the model they must conform to; that is, in order to practise the evangelical charity of our Redeemer and dear and holy humility. Ah! my Sisters and daughters, for charity's sake keep yourselves very low, if you want one day to be great in Paradise, the one goal of all our labours.7 Yes, my Jesus, no other motive leads us to live this life but your love. One day to see you and enjoy you face to face: that is our glory, that is everything. Yes, I tell you, dear daughters, our centre, our happiness! Ah! To have this, as you well know, nothing else is needed but to despise everything that belongs to the world and to see and live everything for Jesus.

  8. Often remember to imitate the charity of your Mother Saint Anne.8 True charity towards one's neighbour. To love those who suffer, to suffer with them, to love one another with one heart, and your Superior as Jesus, because you must see her in the figure of your Spouse. So imagine: if he gave you orders, what obedience would you not show? Well, he commands you through your Superior.

  9. Courage, my dears, pray much, laugh little, always try to keep to yourselves; pray much and meditate a great deal, for you always have the means to meditate: seeing Jesus in the sick, how easy you will find meditation on the passion of Jesus!9

10. My Superior, do you perhaps need anything? Please write and tell me, and I will do all I can at once to send you what you want.

Goodbye, dear daughters. God bless you, and you, Superior, believe me

always your Mother Rosa

1 Carlotta was at the Royal Institute for the Deaf and Dumb in Milan.

2 M. Rosa's mother, Signora Adelaide Campanella.

3 Caterina Rapallino suffered from bronchial asthma, so the remedy did her harm, making it hard for her to breathe.

4 The Spiritual Exercises, in preparation for the feast of Saint Anne, the taking and renewal of Vows and the «clothing» (entry into the Novitiate).

5 She had decided that on that day some of them would receive the religious habit.

6 Fr. Luigi Cogrossi.

7 The eschatological dimension is very strong in Mother Rosa. She expresses it often in her letters, with varying emphases and nuances.

8 The charism of Saint Anne's presence is taking shape in that charity which becomes human closeness, a mother's love that takes on the suffering of those one loves and serves.

9 Mother Rosa meditated assiduously on Christ's passion and had prescribed it for her daughters too.

She answers the letters received and gives news. Suggestions about the bursar. She sends greetings and asks for news of various people.

A.M.F.

My Superior, dear to Jesus

  1. Here I am with you to answer all your dear letters. It is all over; our celebrations went marvellously2 and when I come I will tell you everything.

  2. How it pains me not to be sure that what I write to you will not be read! May the will of Jesus be done, the beginning and end of all we do!

  3. As you know, my health gets worse from one day to the next; indeed during the novena of our dear Mother I was in bed, you might say, for six days. Now I am up, but only just; the swelling, you know, keeps getting worse.

  4. Let us leave these gloomy thoughts and come to you, dear Superior. You did not understand what I said about the Bursar in my last letter. I wanted, first, that at the beginning of each month he should give you an advance on the hospital expenses. You see, my dear, everyone used to do it; because it does not suit us otherwise. The money we keep spending is dead money for us,3 do you understand? Do not be upset; look, dear, these words are just suggestions, and then I leave you free to do as you think best. I would not want this to trouble you. The other thing was that you should tell the Bursar that, if he wished, I would send him pears and lint.

  5. Now tell the Manager that I am very eager for a letter from him, since I cannot come for the present. Given the heat and my poor health it would be too great a strain. I assure you that my weakness is

extreme; my voice is weak because I am short of breath; I hope that when it gets a little cooler I will be able to set out and be with you.

  1. Then, my dear, here in Piacenza we have the cholera, which is striking hard, and we hope to go to the hospital too. God grant it. On the tenth I will send for Carlottina, because the Director has warned me, on account of the cholera. You see, my dear, how many things there are.4

  2. Tell the Canon too,5 who had promised to write to me but I have seen nothing, that I am eager to have a letter from him, and that he should write; tell him why I am not coming, and not to forget to make a memento for me at Mass, his most unworthy penitent.

  3. What are our dear creatures, the girls, doing now? Are they well? I hope so; and tell my Nunciata6 to be calm and cheerful, for I will write her many things privately. What can I say, it is wretched to know that your letters may be opened; if I did not have this fear, I would write you something funny about Fr. Luigi. He is a canon now; the rest I will tell you in person.

  4. Has Bernardi come back? If he comes, make him pay you; it must be months by now.7 They say that whoever is a fool had better stay at home. Patience! It will serve for another time. What is Fr. Paolo doing? Greet him for me. Likewise Signora Irene, Graziella, the doctor, everyone. Is Giuseppe still angry?

Goodbye, my dear. Likewise my beloved girls, whom I embrace in the Heart of Jesus,

and I call myself yours and theirs for ever, Mother Rosa

10. P.S. God bless you and pour into you the true spirit of charity and love towards your neighbour and Jesus. I would send you fruit, but the carriage costs more than the fruit. If you need anything, write and tell me, and I will send you everything.

A.M.F.

My dear Superior

  1. In my profound nothingness I take up my pen to write to you in reply to your long-awaited letter. I can assure you it was a real consolation to me; but, as you well know,1 my rule is never to rejoice too much in satisfactions, and instead to try to find true joy in the adversities and crosses that Jesus sends us and, as our Master, teaches us.

  2. Yes, my dear, if we want to learn this, we must keep before our eyes this mirror, the figure of the Redeemer, and continually look at our own figure in him. With so true a model, I assure you, everything comes to fit us perfectly.2

  3. Be sure to recommend to your daughters that they keep him always before them, so that they may conform their minds and such sublime [teachings] to true holiness, practising the charity I have so often recommended and which our dear Mother Saint Anne teaches us, a virtue in which she so greatly excelled.3

  4. Ah, dear Superior, I assure you that just writing these two lines about charity, I feel a strong desire in me, and to do what? My God, calm this in me, for it makes me suffer too much. Ah! When will the day come when I can give vent to this great longing of mine?4 What am I doing? Superior, forgive me! But what can I say: when this thought seizes my mind I cannot contain it.

  5. I would have a great many things to say, but I must leave them, because they are waiting for me and I could not resume writing until after lunch, and I am afraid of being judged cruel, as I deserve.5

6. All is well and we are in perfect peace. Everything is falling into place marvellously. I am well; the baths are doing me a great deal of good. Write to me. I recommend that you always keep humble and that you pray, and have others pray, for me to the great Saint, our dear Mother.

Receive, and share with your daughters, your Mother's holy Blessing.

Believe me your Rosa Gattorno 6

1 The formal «lei» used by the Mother is surprising; she certainly adopted it to conform to the norms of religious life given to the Sisters by Fr. Tornatore.

2 The mirror. A symbolic image expressing the intentional relationship with Christ, the aspiration to reflect in one's own conscience his reality and sublime holiness, «his model». His perfection is reflected in us and transforms us; «it makes us beautiful», she says elsewhere.

Report on the conduct of Fr. Luigi Cogrossi at the Mother House.

Most Reverend Excellency,

  1. My conscience would be too uneasy if I did not come, with these ill-connected lines but in all truth, as I have always done in the past, to reveal to you with sorrow the bad conduct of that Priest about whom we had long conversations with Your Excellency more than once.1

  2. Ah! If only I had listened to Your Most Reverend Excellency and made the enquiries that were due;2 but, as if steeped in the most abject ignorance there could be, two years ago I lived in the utmost delusion, until by God's mercy his conduct was revealed almost, one might say, all at once; and now3, as is my duty, I come to give you an account of it, partly written by the complainants themselves (as you will see) and partly by me, concerning the irascibility he showed during the time I had to deal with him more closely in this holy Work of the Lord.

  3. All this, Most Reverend Excellency, I leave in your most prudent hands, that you may make of it the use you wisely make in all your undertakings, confident of a holy and wise outcome, as I have always experienced.

  4. I earnestly beg you to keep my name hidden, and on this I rest easy, knowing Your Most Reverend Lordship's integrity.

I respectfully kiss your hand, sure that I shall have a reply from you to this letter. Asking your blessing, I beg you to believe me Your Most Reverend Excellency's

most humble Sr. Anna M. Rosa Gattorno

1 Fr. Luigi Cogrossi had a reputation as a healer and worker of miracles. Though pious and zealous, he had «fanciful, visionary and exaggerated ideas»;

he was therefore admonished by the Holy Office. Cf. Frati Sr. A. Roberta, in Virga Jesse, 1987, 6.

2 The Foundress acknowledges that she should have been more cautious about Cogrossi, but his behaviour had given her no reason to shake the high opinion of his holiness she had long held.

3 That is: he showed himself clearly by his conduct, of which I now come to give you some account, enclosing a report written by the members of the community and another written by me about his «irascibility».

She reports that Fr. Luigi Cogrossi has been dismissed from the Institute.

Most Reverend Eminence,

  1. With the deepest sorrow I come, in conscience bound, to inform Your Most Reverend Eminence that Cogrossi is no longer part of this poor Institute. Everything was done with the knowledge of the Ecclesiastical Superiors.1

  2. I retract all the enthusiasm and assurances of holiness I ventured to express to Your Most Reverend Eminence. Now, in great sorrow, I must confess my ignorance in never having realised that this man was anything but a Saint, as I saw confirmed by the Holy See (Ecclesiastical) on two occasions.2

  3. I do not dare tell you the reasons now, but if you want any clarification, please apply to my Spiritual Father, whom by God's grace I took as soon as I came to Piacenza and whom Your Eminence will surely know by his reputation and learning: Professor Tornatore, Priest of the Mission at San Lazzaro, brother of the Superior in Rome3 at the College at Montecitorio. He will give you every clarification.

  4. I will only say to Your Eminence that I cannot find words enough to thank the Most High for having preserved the whole Community and me, a very poor creature, from the claws of so ferocious a wolf. We owe all this to our dear Mother Saint Anne, who guarded us so well.

  5. I am sure you will favour me with a reply, in which I know I shall find comfort at so painful a time, assuring me of your prayers for this poor sinner, most unworthy of any good, who deserves only to be reviled and insulted by everyone.

With my forehead to the ground I await your Apostolic blessing, professing myself Your Most Reverend Eminence's

most wretched Servant Sr. Anna M. Rosa Gattorno

1 Cf. previous letter.

2 It was known that he had been subjected to disciplinary measures by the Holy Office.

3 Domenico Tornatore. Cf. Letter 156, n. 3; 198.

She tells her that she has dismissed Fr. Luigi Cogrossi. She has sent fruit and other things.

Dear Superior,

  1. Today I received your dear letter together with the Canon's, which, I assure you, came just in time amid the saddest upheavals. I have dismissed Fr. Luigi1 and we no longer have superiors, nor will you ever have them again. Only the Pope and the Bishop will be your Superiors. You are and always will be free. When I arrive I will tell you everything. I can only tell you that I have suffered as it pleased dear Jesus, and I hope this will go towards the remission of my sins. I am still suffering exceedingly, but I am content.

  2. My beloved daughters, dear Superior, God bless you all; I do not and never will cease praying for you, that God may make you Saints, and great Saints. Pray for me. I would go on at greater length in a thousand expressions of the thanks and gratitude I feel towards all of you, but my stomach and the very late hour tonight prevent me.2

  3. The Bursar will receive a sack of pears and a large basket of fruit, which they will divide in three; I have done everything in order, so you need say nothing. I am only letting you know so that you are aware and can act accordingly. I put the Bursar's address on everything; if it should come into your hands, say that it is not yours and have it taken to the Bursar; one of the three shares is for the doctor and the pharmacist, so that you will not be under any obligation to them.3 Inside the sack of pears I put two little parcels for you: the veils, which Rosa will iron, because they had no time here, and stockings for Nunciata.

Goodbye, dear to Jesus and exceedingly dear to me.

Believe me ever your most loving Mother

4. P.S. All four little boots were packed together; the loss must surely have happened on the Railway.

1 Canon: cf. Letter 14, n. 7; saddest upheavals: on account of Cogrossi, so that it had been necessary to act energetically with the radical decision to remove him and to inform the ecclesiastical authorities. Cf. Letters 21 and 22.

2 Neither tiredness nor illness prevented her from offering her daughters gestures of free and grateful love.

3 Giving the fruit as a gift was a sign of generosity and of sharing the gifts the good God offered her in abundance in the large kitchen garden of the Mother House. For the names cf. Letter 14, n. 8.

She says she is honoured to correspond with an exemplary person, of deep spirituality and zealous in charity.

Very Reverend Superior,

  1. Out of obedience2 I set down on this paper some ill-connected characters3 and a few words of comfort, for my wretched tongue [is not] equal to a person such as yourself, whose heart is versed in heavenly sublimities.

  2. I can therefore only raise feeble prayers to the Most High in thanksgiving for such signal benefits, and for leaving here below among us mortals creatures of such exemplary life and learning.

  3. How dear to the Author of all good are the labours, the toil, the tedium of long conversations with people of either sex, from which Your Reverence is accustomed to draw those great benefits that flash like a dream through the mind of this wretched creature; but so great is her misery and so slight her understanding that she cannot make them a subject of discourse.

  4. You surely, O Creator, keep giving me dealings with your beloved creatures, so that this weakened servant of yours may lean on the favourable prayers of these persons, that they may support her and keep her from falling into an abyss of errors.

  5. How glad I was to spend time with a soul who works in the Saviour's vineyard; I can only rejoice and beg you to keep me in a corner of your heart and to believe me, as I truly am, the most unworthy of all creatures.4

Your most humble Sr. Anna Maria Rosa Gattorno

1 Sister of Fr. Giovanni Battista Tornatore and a religious of the Daughters of Our Lady of the Garden (known as Gianelline), she was at that time superior of the community at Ventimiglia. She joined the Daughters of Saint Anne in 1879. Cf. Letter 25, n. 3.

2 She was certainly writing on Fr. Tornatore's advice, which for her was a duty of obedience.

3 Not well connected.

4 This letter is a draft and therefore not very clearly written.

She thanks her for her reply. She looks forward to her niece joining the Daughters of Saint Anne.

Reverend Superior,

  1. My indisposition, which kept me in bed for some days and from which I have not yet recovered, was the only reason for my delay in thanking you for the pleasure I felt on receiving your most esteemed letter.

  2. Your letter was certainly dear and precious to me; but it pained me just as much to read the title of Superior1 which you give me. I should like to correct you and beg you not to give me that title again, for I am only a poor Daughter of Saint Anne and never a Superior; indeed I live under obedience to the Superior of this House.2

  3. I heard with inexpressible pleasure the news that a dear niece of yours will soon be among my daughters; I cannot express to you the joy I felt, nor can I tell you how eagerly I await her, and the other two as well.3

  4. I thank you for all you are doing for this poor Institute. I am and always will be most grateful to you. Please accept my warmest thanks. Keep me in a corner of your heart, offering fervent prayers to God for me.

Do not forget me, and believe me

your most humble Sr. Anna Maria Rosa Gattorno

1 She was giving her the title of Superior General.

2 This house.

3 Of the three nieces, daughters of her brother Andrea, Rosa, who was ready to embrace religious life, apparently with the Daughters of Saint Anne, entered her aunt's Congregation instead in 1869. The other two entered the Daughters of Saint Anne: Maddalena in 1876, taking the name Sr. A. Giuseppina, and Giovanna in 1879, Sr. A. Vincenza. In that same year, 1879, their aunt Maria Teresa also moved from the Congregation of the Daughters of Our Lady of the Garden to the Daughters of Saint Anne.

She suggests that she ask the hospital Administration for a period of rest in Piacenza for health reasons.

A.M.F.

Good Superior,

dear to Jesus, my beloved Superior,

  1. God bless you, dear creature; I cannot find words enough to express to you, with the liveliest feeling of gratitude, what your dear words meant to me. Rest assured that this very poor Mother of yours, as long as she lives, will never cease to pray God to make you holy and grant you everything; when I am dead, if I go to a place of salvation, I will do the same.1

  2. My dear, I am making an effort to write to you in my own hand, which I assure you is tiring for me, because, as you will have heard from this dear Superior, your sister2 — though I would have been far from writing it to you myself — my health is bad. She thought it best [to write and tell you] so that you would know why I have been delayed in coming to Cento.

  3. Dear Superior, I am afraid you are overtiring yourself, and if you think fit to ask the Manager for some help for a time, while you are so burdened with patients, do ask, and if it is granted I will send you a good creature at once and you will be pleased; they will not have to spend anything.3

  4. For charity's sake, write and tell me about the health situation. Is the cholera threatening you at all? If it were, you could let it be known that you would be ready to provide nurses, meaning that I would send them to you from here; you will let this be heard indirectly.4

  5. Dear Superior, what could you ever have done to me? Nothing; I assure you that your words brought tears to my eyes; never write such things to me again; just ask, and you shall have everything.5

  1. As for the collars, if you agree, I will bring them myself, and also the bodice

for Rosa. I sent some that were already begun; if you cannot do them, have the dressmaker finish them; if you want others, I will bring them.6

  1. Dear Superior, what can I say: now I seem to be recovering, but I have my little girl with me and do not know how I can manage to come until her Director calls her back.7 If you would like to come with someone else for the feast of Saint Francis, I could do this: send your sister along with another, good at keeping accounts, for a week, if you like the idea; see whether the Manager would be happy for you to take this holiday, without saying anything. Do you understand? Do as you wish.8

  2. I assure you that when I thought I was dying I thought of you9 and was grieved to leave you without seeing you. And then, the state I was leaving you in! But the good God preserved me, and I hope I will leave you well settled before I die.10 Tell me a little about practical matters. We are well, as Jesus wills; and you? I cannot write any more, for I am suffering a great deal.

Goodbye, dear Francesca, and greet everyone for me. God bless you, and I am

for ever your Mother Anna

1 Good, dear to Jesus, my beloved... dear creature. These terms express an affectionate bond intensified and refined by shared daily suffering and by the experience of an illness that made her fear the worst: farewell for ever. A bond of motherhood and daughterhood that reaches beyond death.

2 The superior of the Mother House community, Sr. A. Luigia Camisa, one of the five sisters in the first clothing of the Daughters of Saint Anne on 8 December 1866. She was Sr. Francesca Camisa's elder sister.

3 Sr. A. Francesca's health was delicate. In view of the overwork caused by the large number of patients, the Mother suggests a period of rest; she herself would provide a replacement free of charge. The Manager must be consulted; cf. Letter 12, n. 3.

4 Indirectly: after obtaining precise information, and avoiding a direct offer to commit the sisters to wider service.

5 A contest of anticipating love and humility. The Superior is the one who serves.

6 White collars were part of the sisters' habit. She had already sent some that were begun. The Mother was always attentive, even in the smallest things: if you cannot, have the dressmaker finish them.

7 This is Carlotta, who had been with her since 10 August (cf. Letters 14 and 19).

8 The clothing ceremony for several postulants, including those of the Cento community, had been fixed for the feast of Saint Francis, 4 October. The Mother fully respects her daughter's choice.

9 I remembered you.

10 The thought of her Family, growing ever larger, makes her relive the great suffering of the days when she thought she was leaving them. She vividly expresses a mother's grief: without seeing you... the state I was leaving you in! A little over a year after the foundation, the institution lacked any legal security. She was its only pivot.

She has sent fruit and asks for acknowledgement. Expressions of concern and solicitude.

A.M.F.

  1. I have sent you a sack of pears with walnuts, and also a basket for Fr. Paolo. Let me know as soon as you receive them.

  2. I am sorry to learn from the girls' letters that you have lost your voice; for charity's sake take care of yourself, do not fret, because, my dear, you know well that we are in this tearful vale.1 I assure you that suffering, suffering alone, is our inheritance.

  3. Dear, I pray Jesus to give all this to me and relieve all of you. Only to me, because, I assure you, it is very dear to me and I have no other treasure on this earth but suffering. Yes, you are my treasure.2

Goodbye, dear. God bless you all, and drink deep from the cup of suffering.

I am, of our Mother Saint Anne, the most wretched Mother Rosa

1 Pain and daily setbacks are inevitable. To accept them peacefully, «actively», rather than endure them «fretfully» (= with a reaction of anxiety), is wisdom.

2 Yes, you are my treasure. She is addressing «suffering» directly.

She asks Jesus to give all the suffering to her and relieve her daughters, still little, unable to find «joy» in it. Suffering is her only treasure: she has discovered it, loves it, and it belongs to her.

They are not to leave Cento. It is better for her to go there.

Dearest Superior,

  1. It is high time I answered your dear letter, which I received the day before yesterday; but if you knew the reason for the delay you would certainly agree with me. You see, hearing that you were preparing to come1 with Eufemia gave me great pleasure, but I could not make up my mind to take your sister2 away from here; and besides, a very vivid thought kept coming to me, and I said to myself, and then spoke of it to the Father3 and the Superior: send a new face down there? You know what sort of people they are; I fear they might take it badly; so I decided to leave the girl and come myself with Caterina.4 That is the decision.

  2. Indeed I will come before you. Everything is happening at once: Countess Castelnuovo,5 whom Anna Maria Rosa knows, is coming on Friday to stay here for several days, so as soon as she leaves I will come.

  3. Pray that the Lord will send me the means to come, for this too is a big obstacle: for four people to go and return it costs 120 [francs]. You see that it is no small expense at a time like this. I assure you it worries me.6 Patience; I would not want to discourage you now that I have confided this to you, but you will take it with patience and resignation, thanking the Lord who wishes to humble us in this way.7

I close, my dear, because my head aches badly.

Receive a handshake from your very poor Mother, as she implores the Lord's holy blessing on you, and I am

your Mother as long as I live, Anna Maria Rosa

1 You are getting ready to come.

2 Sr. A. Luigia Camisa, superior of the Mother House community.

3 Fr. Tornatore.

4 Caterina Rapallino (cf. Letter 6). Leave the girl, that is, Carlotta.

5 Adele Castelnuovo, her friend and a benefactor of the Institute. Cf. her letters to M. Rosa, Arch St FSA, pos. Amiche (cf. Letters 93 and 169).

6 The religious Family had no fixed income; it lived «trusting in Providence», on people's spontaneous offerings and on «begging» for alms.

7 «Discourage you»: dishearten you. Hardship is an occasion for growth in humility and in trust in God the Father.

She expresses her sorrow over the two sick sisters and gives her spiritual advice and news.

A.M.F.

Dear Superior,

  1. I was intensely grieved to learn that Daria and Eufemia are ill. The Lord wants to humble us in everything. As for a doctor, I would turn to the physician of all our good, our Mother Saint Anne. She will make them well; and then I would give Daria a small spoonful of the oil I left you, and when Eufemia has a nosebleed she should anoint her nose and then say three Our Fathers, Hail Marys and Glory Bes to the Most Holy Trinity.1 Dear Superior, keep me always informed about their health.

  2. Tell me: how are you managing now with the Bursar about money; does he give you an advance? I hope you have done as you were told. Look, my dear, you will see that this poor Mother of yours is giving you good advice; I hope you will not take these words badly.2

  3. If you have in mind to stay and wait for me, I will come as soon as I have taken Carlotta to Milan.3 I will come and stay a long time; and then I think I will come so that you can rest, and you can do as you like: come here or stay near me, making a little retreat, while I do everything with Caterina; are you happy with that?4

  4. Open your heart to me with complete frankness, as I do to you, your very poor mother, who once again feels unwell and is weighed down by the burdens and charges of this poor house.5 Yes, my dear, I recommend you always to keep yourself humbled. Ah! We can never be furnished enough with this [virtue]; and blessed are we if we could be trampled on by everyone! We are never so loved by our Jesus as when, in the world's eyes, we appear useless and despised creatures.6

It is late now and I still have much to write; so, imploring a thousand blessings from Heaven upon you, which I wish the Lord to share among all of you,

I remain ever your Mother Rosa

1 Olive oil which she had blessed following an inspiration received in prayer.

2 She tactfully and gently repeats the advice of Letter 15.

3 Cf. Letter 14, n. 2, and Letters 19, 26 and 28.

4 She wants to replace her personally. She is bringing Caterina Rapallino, the young woman who is discerning her own call to the Daughters of Saint Anne and is strongly opposed by her parents.

5 The burdens of the Piacenza house were enormous; consider only the debt to be repaid to Teresa Porta. Cf. Letters 31, 32, 33.

6 Humility! She never tires of instilling it. Here we hear an echo of the «perfect joy» of her «dear Father Saint Francis», whom she had followed as a tertiary, making her profession on 24.9.1861.
Letters are going astray. She repeats the recommendations of the previous letter, which did not reach its addressee.

She sends the document requested of her.

  1. I am sending you the receipt you asked me for.2 It was drawn up by someone who knows about the loan you made to this house. I have copied it out myself and am sending it to you to satisfy your wish.

  2. Please give my regards to your excellent mother.

With greetings, I am your most unworthy Servant

Sr. Anna Maria Rosa

1 She is replying to a letter from the addressee dated 20 September.

Piacenza. Mother House. The façade.

She tries to make her understand her personal difficulties and those of the house.

Dear Teresa,

  1. What can this wretched sinner answer you, lacking words that might bring you, my friend, peace and tranquillity?1 I can only repeat what I have already told you.

  2. You have known my circumstances not just from now but from before there was any talk of your loan to this very poor house.2 I entrust myself to your good judgement and to the will of God, in whom I place everything.

  3. Now, if my Jesus wishes to play with me in this way,3 I bow my head, as to something I deserve. I only pray the Most High to grant this skeleton strength and patience to bear everything in peace.

At the feet of Jesus I call myself your very poor Servant Rosa

1 Appealing to their deep friendship, Mother Rosa tries to dispel her creditor's distrust, repeating that she would repay the sum owed.

2 With these words she alludes to the purpose of the loan: the founding of the religious institution, an ideal Teresa had shared. The money had therefore been lent not to the Foundress personally but to the House. The Mother holds firm to this principle, drawing also on her father's advice (cf. letter of Francesco Gattorno, 17.9.67). Teresa, however, insists: «I did not lend to the house, but to you» (letter of 20.9.67).

3 Inasmuch as he permits such suffering and pain.

She assures her that she will settle with her as soon as possible by paying the debt.

My dear Teresa,

  1. I am sorry to keep repeating the same thing to you, for I know very well that I am wearying you.

  2. God knows I would not wish to cause you the slightest annoyance, but what can I do? You know our circumstances and knew them already,1 and you have proof in hand that this house would by no means wish to harm your children, given the good faith in which you placed your trust.2

  3. Since you handed over the money, I reply that it is our wish to repay you as soon as possible.

  4. If you insist and are determined to damage our common cause,3 ignorant of business as I am, I will refer you to my Father, so that he may deal with you as he thinks best.

I am the most wretched Anna Rosa

5. You lent your money to this house of the Lord, and far from refusing, the House is ready to give you the fullest guarantee; so it seems to me this difficulty has been smoothed over, and you can live calm and secure about your children's interests.4 I let you know that on Sunday we have exposition of the Blessed Sacrament.

Goodbye. Greet your Mother for me.5

I am your most unworthy Servant

Rosa

1 Having worked on the foundation at the start, she knows the poverty of the House well.

2 If she will restore her former trust, she can be sure that her children will suffer no financial harm. The money will be returned to her as soon as possible.

3 The creditor wanted to put a mortgage on the Palazzo Dal Verme (cf. her letter of 25.9.67) and threatened legal action. To avoid this, Mother Rosa proposes entrusting the matter to her father. The question was closed by a settlement. Cf. Arch St FSA, A. 3. 37, Mmv 43.

4 Another reassuring word and an invitation to meet again in prayer before him who is the centre of unity and the source of peace.

5 Maria Pezzi, widow Porta. Arch St FSA, pos Amiche, 11.

She declares her readiness to take in, maintain and educate the cholera orphans in her community.

Most Illustrious Sir,

1. The undersigned hastens to inform Your Lordship that, after mature reflection, she cannot but accede to Your wish3 to offer shelter to those poor little girls left orphans in the last outbreak of cholera,4 and that she is glad not only to give them a home but also to provide them with suitable board, convinced that Your Lordship and the citizens you administer will appreciate5 this effort, inspired by a feeling of Christian charity and compassion and by the desire to be of some use to a City that has given her proofs of goodwill and trust.6

The undersigned takes this favourable opportunity to renew to you the expression of her deep respect.

Your Most Illustrious Lordship's most humble Rosa Gattorno

5 Will know how to value.

She will write to the bursar. She is sending two baskets of fruit.

A.M.F.

Dearest Superior,

  1. From your letter, which I found enclosed in one from the Marquis, the Manager,1 I see that all my letters have reached you and none was lost. I think it is your great longing for my letters, so that two days seem like a hundred years to you: so, my dear, that is how it is.

  2. Now I will see to writing a letter to show the Bursar, and then next month he will give you an advance.2

  3. Meanwhile I am sending Fr. Paolo a basket of winter pears, and some to you too. Mention to Signora Irene, I mean in passing, in conversation, to see whether they would be welcome; then, when I send the pears, I would also give some to the Bursar, and take the opportunity to make this remark to him.

  4. I am delighted about our Daria. So I will come without fail at the end of October and stay as long as God pleases.

Greet everyone for me, and try to be the servants of all; of all. I hope you received my letter through the Canon.3 Please greet everyone for me, and I am

your Mother Rosa Gattorno

5. P.S. God bless you, dear daughters, and believe me, until eternity, your Mother, your tenderly most loving Mother Rosa.4

1 Cf. Letter 12, n. 3.

2 The bursar, Signor Carlo Leonesi, did not care for the subject of an advance on expenses. She will write to him and send him the pears as a gift (fruit from the garden that was, and still is, beside the Mother House), with a note. Cf. Letters 15, 3 and 19, 4.

3 Humility towards all in service, which is an expression of love. The Mother passes from the singular to the plural, addressing all the sisters. The Canon is Fr. Michele Vaccari.
