She urges her to be generous, sketching the spiritual profile of a Daughter of Saint Anne.

A.M.F.

My dear Superior,

  1. When will the day come when you are a true daughter of our great Mother Saint Anne?1 A daughter of this great woman thinks only of serving her in the office and the place where Jesus has put her, and is attached to nothing and to no one. Why do you always show such attachment to my person and long so much for me to come there? You tell me that by God's goodness things are going well; so is it necessary for me to come a little sooner rather than later?2

  2. On the other hand, my presence is needed here these days for the interests of our Institute and of our Mother Saint Anne. Courage, my daughter, show yourself a generous daughter of our Mother Saint Anne, a daughter detached from everything, a daughter who seeks nothing but the interest, the pleasure and the glory of her Mother, the great Saint. She can accept as daughters only generous hearts who for love of her are ready to go anywhere, stay anywhere, and suffer everything for Jesus.3

  3. As soon as our Mother permits, I will come at once to relieve you, and that will be in a few days, my dear daughter. I hope you will accept what I write as words entirely of our dear Mother Saint Anne, who loves you with all her heart.

  4. As I write to you, your Mother is in the guest quarters with the Superior, your mother and your two sisters, and a little niece. Dear, they are having lunch; you will not believe it: this poor Mother of yours had barely taken a little food and went straight to her desk.

  5. I can hardly write any more. I am exceedingly tired, all day and part of the night.

  6. We have the deaf-mute girls at risk, the hearing girls at risk, and the others.4

  7. Dear, if you could see this poor Mother of yours! I think I must be a skeleton, for judging by the surprise I cause everyone I must be frightening.5 Ah! If only I frightened the devil too, so that when I am dead he will have nothing to do with me.

Tell me about practical matters, and

believe me your most loving Mother Rosa

8. I have not yet sent you the pears, but I will soon. Goodbye. Greet everyone for me; I will soon be with you.

1 The expressions about Saint Anne repeat Fr. Tornatore word for word: «great Woman... great Saint».

2 She points out the inconsistency: «if things are going well», why «is it necessary for me to come a little sooner?».

3 My daughter, show yourself a daughter of Saint Anne. Here is her face: generous, detached, seeking only the interest, pleasure and glory of the holy Mother; ready to stay or go anywhere and to suffer everything for Jesus.

4 The deaf-mute girls at risk. The first two had arrived in Piacenza on 25 September 1867; others soon followed. Cf. Fiocchi A. M., op. cit., I, p. 167. Cf. Letter 38, 5.

5 The number of Daughters and of those in their care was growing, and so were the tasks and worries. And she gave herself entirely, to the point of exhaustion.

She comforts her, speaking of the love of the holy Mother Saint Anne, and gives her spiritual advice. She confides her own worries about the poverty of the Mother House. Other news.

Dear Superior,

  1. Here I am back from Milan, soon to return to [...], where we have taken a house for our Institute.1

  2. Dear to Jesus, be of good heart, for your Mother Saint Anne loves you and takes account of all the sufferings and desolation her Daughter endures, keeping refreshment ready which in due time she will not delay to send you. Now, my dear, is the time to suffer, if one day we want to have a beautiful joy.2 Our father Saint Francis of Assisi used to say: «so great is the good I hope for that every pain is a delight to me». I assure you that if your suffering could be passed on, I would take it all, all of it, on myself, to give you back the happiness you long for. My dear, that happiness is not found among the living on earth but among the living of Eternity, those who tomorrow3 will sing his glories in that blessed abode of Paradise.

  3. As for the great dryness you are suffering, I assure you that if you are resigned, your Mother Saint Anne will console you when you least expect it; and I, your very poor Mother, but full of affection for her daughter Francesca, whom every day she clasps in the heart of her spouse Jesus, to obtain from this wound a true absorption of every earthly thing, that she may come out of it purified by so great a balm.4

  4. My dear daughter, believe this poor Mother of yours, who keeps you always at her side wherever she goes; whatever blessing she receives, she always says to her Jesus: «Beloved of my heart, make this creature wholly holy for me!» And how many things I say to him in the morning, and how many I

have said to him, for my Francesca! Ah, dear daughter, listen: be of good heart and believe that you will soon be comforted.5

  1. As for the bodices,6 I think it better that you buy them if you need them, because, dear Francesca, you see that sending them costs more; and besides, we are now so short of means that I do not know whether I am coming or going.7 Everyone makes fine promises, but when it comes to deeds no one is to be seen. You, who run a small household yourself, can tell me what a sorry business this is.

  2. Dear to Jesus and beloved by me, here we have managed as best we could with rags to protect ourselves from the cold; you see, and always hoping in the Lord's mercy that he will not send cold weather, for I assure you it is a real predicament.8

  3. Now I am soon leaving for this town, where another house is being planted, and then for Milan, where they are already buying a house.9 I cannot stay any longer now, for I have endless things to do.

Pray and have others pray, and receive [the greetings] of one who calls herself with all affection

your poor but loving Mother, Sr. Anna Maria Rosa Gattorno

  1. If you have not yet used the veil I brought you, I would like you to send it back to me, because I need it for Angiola,10 who has to wear a hat, and I could not buy one for now. Soon I will send you a little present for the doctor, to keep his feet warm,11 and something for Graziella; inside I will put some veils, which I assure you are lovely; the ones I told you I had had dyed.

  2. Warm regards to the Manager and to everyone. Dear, about the things I said I would send you, you will say I do not keep my word. It grieves me, but what can I do if we have not bought what you want? I do not speak to you of thrift, for I have had too many proofs of yours, so I know how dear to your heart is your house in Piacenza, so poor and so full of troubles.

Receive an embrace and believe me once again your most loving Mother. Later I will write to Framesta.12 Be so kind as to tell us.

1 The name of the place is missing; M. Rosa left the space blank, evidently intending to fill it in later because she could not recall it at the moment. It is Cerro Maggiore (Milan), as appears from Letters 47 and 49.

2 It is the time to suffer: a phrase dear to Mother Rosa, often found in her letters. Sharing in Jesus' sacrifice is an eschatological sharing in joy without end.

3 4 October, feast of Saint Francis of Assisi.

4 True absorption: the mystical experience of feeling deep within the transforming touch of his presence.

5 Closeness, being united in Christ's love, is a source of consolation.

6 The sisters' undergarments.

7 Whether I am coming or going: with so many mouths to feed (cf. Letters 36, 6 and 38, 5), debts were piling up and suppliers were demanding payment.

8 They thus lived in extreme poverty, trusting in Providence and praying that it would not turn very cold.

9 That is, Cerro Maggiore. In Milan Fr. Eliseo Ghislandi, director of the «Royal Institute for the Deaf and Dumb», where Mother Rosa's daughter Carlotta was a pupil, was working to found a work for deaf-mute girls «already educated» in other Institutes and sent back by them to their families. He was in negotiations with Mother Rosa.

10 Angela Degrossi was, as already noted, one of M. Rosa's first companions. She had to go out because she was attending the course for the elementary-school teaching qualification. Cf. Letter 38, 5.

11 To keep his feet warm. These gestures of thoughtfulness and delicacy radiate the love Rosa lived with an intensity of total self-giving, excluding no one. The doctor is Dr Didaco Facchini; Graziella, his daughter.

12 It is not known who this is.

She expresses her sorrow for the Sisters who are suffering from the cold. Let her obtain clothing to protect them. Important news about the Mother House.

A.M.F.

Dear Superior,

  1. A few moments ago I received your dear letter along with two others; I do not know whose they are, because they are not signed.

  2. How sorry I am to hear that you are cold! My Jesus, give them your fire, and they will be warm!1 Dear Francesca, I thought all the quilts were there. If any are missing, tell the Bursar. And besides, don't you all have shawls? Tell the Bursar also to provide you with winter clothes, little jackets, as we had agreed, and the blankets. For charity's sake, wrap up warm!2

  3. Write and tell me in detail what I should bring you for the cold, and I will bring it at once: whether bodices, skirts, whatever you mean; and if you can buy what you want there, do so, and I will be happy.3

  4. Write and tell me whether the Superior of the brothers has come again.4 In a few days I will be with you; but, my dear, what can I say: if you knew how much work there is here, you certainly would not even write asking me to come.

  5. As I told you before, we have begun taking in hearing girls at risk, deaf-mutes, and girls who have already fallen. I have no rest.5 Angiola is studying to become a qualified teacher so that she can do her course; soon we are opening the day schools.6 Dear one of my Jesus, I have also had a lot of trouble with Teresa.7 I will tell you everything when I come. So you see I can say that I am tearing myself away from my labours to please you. Dear, I really do not know whether I am coming or going, I am so immersed in the tangles of this house.

  6. Each time you receive my letters, let me know; have

the shoes I wore last year mended for me. I will bring you the veils and the neckbands,8 and I will let you know the day I leave, because I am making it all one journey. I am going to Milan to take Carlotta and then coming to Cento.9

Greet all my dear daughters for me, and Signora Irene and Graziella too. Caterina sends her greetings, as does the Superior, who is here with me.

Goodbye, and believe me your most loving Mother Rosa

1 The outward cold reminds her of a far more dangerous cold, and she invokes the fire of Jesus' love upon her daughters.

2 She is painfully surprised, because she was convinced that they all had quilts against the cold at night and heavy clothing for the day, as she had agreed with the bursar.

3 What is needed must be provided at once: she will provide it herself, or else it is to be bought regardless of expense.

4 Cf. Letter 10, n. 3.

5 Cf. Letter 36, 6.

6 Cf. Letter 37, n. 10. Note the Mother's organisational foresight in giving the sisters professional training.

7 Teresa Porta. Cf. Letters 6, n. 7; 12, n. 2; 31, 32, 33.

8 Neckbands: part of the Sisters' habit, to which the collar was sewn.

9 Carlotta was still in Piacenza with the Mother. (Cf. Letters 14, n. 2; 18, 2; 19, 6, etc.).

She clarifies her views on the proposals and conditions for the community of Daughters of Saint Anne that was to work for the Patronage for deaf-mute girls in Milan.

Very Reverend Director,

  1. Jesus! What a fine heart you have, to feel so keenly the dangers facing your deaf-mute girls. Ah, how I share your compassion! But for the moment, Director, I cannot tell you to send me the young woman you mention; we shall come to an understanding about that another time.1 Now I reply to the numbered points of your letter.2

  2. On no. 1. I have nothing to object to.3

As to no. 2, I leave it to your kindness to fix the maintenance of my daughters who will come to that house. The Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne, in each of its houses, wants no more than its poor food and clothing, and can then work diligently for the glory of God.

On no. 3. I tell you that in that house there cannot be more of my daughters than the Patronage for deaf-mutes wishes, unless4 there were benefactors there who called them to carry out other works of our Institute. This, it is understood, would have to be without any harm to the Patronage itself.

In no. 4 you ask whether I am prepared to stipulate that, in addition to the Patronage's means, the Daughters of Saint Anne should add their own means, if they have any. I reply that the Institute of Saint Anne's Daughters will have, in all its houses, whatever goods benefactors choose to give them, bound by whatever conditions they choose. So you see, Director, that such a question does not arise. If you want to reassure the benefactors about us, tell them that the Daughters of Saint Anne are not servants but mothers, and therefore, as far as it depends on them, they will not

only preserve the means of the Patronage entrusted to them but increase them, until, were it possible, the time might come when it could take in the whole world.

On nos. 5 and 6 I have nothing to observe; only, if it were not too presumptuous, I would say that I would not put in the programme the words of no. 5, outings to relatives. Likewise the statement in no. 6 that the deaf-mute girls will go walking in fours. On these points experience may in time teach that it is better done otherwise.5

3. That is what I had to tell you, Director. I hope there is nothing in it to displease you, so that this work may begin, which can do so much good to so many poor deaf-mute girls at risk.6

Please give my most distinguished regards to the esteemed Mistresses7 and believe me Your Reverence's

most humble Sr. Anna Maria Rosa Gattorno

1 He had written to her on 10.10.1867 in these words: «only last week a young deaf-mute girl, who had recently left the Institute of the Daughters of Charity and was as good as an angel, had to take refuge in the maternity home. O God! And who knows how many others are in danger!».

2 In which he submits to her a draft plan of the work, so that the final «programme» can be drawn up in full agreement between them.

3 Point 1 stated: «I shall leave the sisters full freedom to keep their rule, but they are not to accept other girls, only deaf-mutes».

4 The Patronage, that is, the association for the benefit of deaf-mute girls, which was then being set up. Senon(ché) nel caso: unless.

5 No. 5 read: «... the deaf-mute girls should be freer than in the school; in short, they should live as if they were at home; so a walk every day if the weather permits, no uniform, outings to relatives, etc.». No. 6: «from this premise follows the need for persons not belonging to the Congregation (of the DSA) to be with the pupils at all times when the sisters have to make their meditation or other devotions, and to accompany the deaf-mute girls on walks in fours, not in a line like schoolgirls. I would not want to see the sisters in the street with the deaf-mutes; people would say they are nuns: they are sacrificed deaf-mutes».

6 By its own statute the Royal Institute for the Deaf and Dumb in Milan was reserved for pupils of «civil condition», that is, from well-to-do families. The new one would also take in poor girls at risk.

7 Carlotta's teachers.

She asks her to support her application for a young woman to be admitted free of charge to the specialist course for teaching the deaf.

Most esteemed Marchioness,

  1. Your charity and kindness, so well known to me, make me bold to turn to you and ask your help, in a matter very close to my heart, in a need in which I now find myself. I hope and trust that you, who have always been so good to me, will not refuse me your assistance in what I am about to ask, which I dare to hope for only from your great kindness.

  2. Since I am obliged to take up the branch of Deaf-Mute girls at risk, I need a Teacher with a diploma. In our house in Piacenza there is a girl with a good education, received from her very well-to-do family,2 but she lacks the diploma, and to obtain it she needs permission from the Ministry of Public Instruction to sit the examination privately, and also admission to a free place at the Royal Institute in Milan, where there are free places for training as Teachers of the Deaf and Dumb.

  3. Only you, most esteemed Marchioness, through your excellent brother, who has such influence with the Ministry, can obtain these two permissions for me, namely to sit the examination privately and to enter the Institute in Milan, the petition for which I enclose.3

  4. Ah yes, if you could obtain so much through your good offices, be assured that neither I nor my Community could ever forget so great a Benefactress and Co-worker in this work of charity. The many proofs of charity I have received from you encourage me to hope that you will exert yourself for this one too, and I assure you that God will know how to reward you.

Trusting to obtain this, I beg you to accept my most distinguished regards and to believe me your

most humble Sr. Anna M. Rosa Gattorno

1 Presumably the Marchioness Fanny Trivulzio, resident in Milan, daughter of Countess Marianna Anguissola d'Altoè, a friend of Mother Rosa. She was very influential. Later she took an active interest in founding in Milan a house for the education of poor girls and home nursing of the sick. Cf. Arch St FSA, Pos. Amiche, letter of Countess Marianna Anguissola of 8 June 1869.

2 Colomba Della Cella.

3 The petition is justified by a notable exception, sitting the examinations privately, and by the difficulty of obtaining a free place at the «School of Method» attached to the Royal Institute, where only three places were reserved for non-paying students.
She has returned from Cento. She asks that a date be fixed for Carlotta's return to the institute in Milan, where she is to take her.

She is about to take Carlotta back to Milan. Let the Manager know that she will be away from Piacenza.

A.M.F.

Dear Superior,

  1. Two lines to keep my word, though they cost me a great deal, as my health is very poor.

  2. Blessed for ever be the will of good Jesus, who gives us such dear suffering.

  3. Let the Marquis, the Manager, know as soon as you can that I am leaving for Milan, having been called by Carlotta's Director to take her back to the School,1 so that if he wanted to come he would not make the journey in vain, as I do not know how long I will stay in Milan.

  4. Tell the daughters to pray for me. Dear Francesca, remember me in the Heart of Jesus, in which I always try to enclose you, and in that dear treasure, the spouse of his beloved ones. Yes, certainly not mine, for I am a sink of sins,2 but yours, blessed Daughters of Saint Anne, our Mother. Surely he will not allow this poor creature to be lost, but will surely let her be converted and die a Christian; God grant it.3

Live faithful to your Rules and obedient, and you will be sure of Paradise.4

God bless you, and believe me your poor Mother, who loves you tenderly in Jesus

Sr. Anna Maria Rosa

5. P.S. That delivery note you have, which reached you 118

when I was there, was still for the sack of pears you had already received.

Greet everyone for me: Graziella, Signora Irene; and tell Graziella that I am seeing to sending her a little box, which will keep my memory always fresh for her. And so to everyone; my regards to the Manager too.

1 The director, Fr. Eliseo Ghislandi.

2 Jesus is the spouse of her beloved daughters, not hers, for she is unworthy; she is «a sink» (= a collecting place) of sins. In the dazzling light of the Spirit she experiences her radical existential misery. She suffers from it, not for her own sake, but for having offended God. But she trusts in God.

3 Physical prostration is accompanied by spiritual sufferings.

4 The Rules, a code of life, guarantee the path of holiness and fidelity to God within the Institute.

She wishes him growth in the love of God and reminds him of their mutual promise to remember each other in prayer.

A.M.F.

Blessed be Jesus

Most esteemed Father Agostino,1

  1. The wine of the Chalice must truly keep you thirsty for you to have so tremendous a burning thirst for it all the time. You are right to long to be inebriated, and I with all affection long to see you drunk with this wine.2

  2. But I would not want this to make dear Father Agostino fly away like Father Bernardo's Angel; but, for the love of the Lord, if it should, ah! come first and fetch this donkey, so that it too may share in Father Agostino's blessed flight.

  3. Go on being faithful to the promise, which for my part I will try never to forget, for all eternity; if good Jesus in his mercy gives me Paradise — undeserved though it is — I will remember the wine and the one who helped me to salvation. Send Father Bernardo to me soon!3

And in the hearts of Jesus and Mary I am your

most humble, most obedient Sr. Anna Maria Rosa Gattorno

1 Father Agostino Donadio, of the Minims of Saint Francis of Paola, was postulator of the cause of beatification of Father Bernardo Maria Clausi.

2 The metaphor and the lightly playful tone of the letter express the deep friendship between these two souls thirsting for God.

3 They shared love and veneration for Father Bernardo, each for specifically personal reasons. For Father Agostino he was the confrere who modelled holiness; for Mother Rosa, the inspirer of the Family of the Daughters of Saint Anne, and her guide.

Cf. Index III, 1.

She urges her to be faithful to Jesus and asks for prayers.

A.M.F.

Caterina, my beloved daughter

(I wish no one to see this)

  1. God bless you and arm you with patience; may the mantle of our holy Mother cover you and hide you from the eyes of the world, so that you may not be stolen from Jesus, your beloved Spouse.1

  2. Your sister is no longer coming;2 I wrote the reason to the Superior. Pray for this poor Mother of yours, who is as the Lord wills.

  3. Today my mind is entirely with you in our Chapel before the dear Blessed Sacrament. Have the little girls pray for what you know of.

  4. Dear little daughter, yes, even though the world wants to tear this name from you, God will confirm it to you.3

Goodbye; I embrace you in the Heart of Jesus, and I am always

your most loving Mother Sr. Anna Maria Rosa

1 Caterina Rapallino (cf. Letter 6) had told her parents of her religious vocation to the Daughters of Saint Anne, but had met with a firm refusal.

2 Caterina's sister Emilia. She too was later a guest at the Mother House.

3 The sentence rings out as strong and sure encouragement for the young woman.

A few lines of encouragement. She will soon answer her letter.

Dear Caterina,

Cheerful on the Cross! It is late and I cannot write to you. I will write another time and answer yours. My dear Daughter, for ever not of men but of Jesus.

I am your

most loving Mother Rosa1

1 A few words, but full of human and spiritual force. They vividly reveal Mother Rosa's personality and her motherly feeling and understanding.

She thanks her for her interest and urges her to support her application for a free place at the Royal Institute for the Deaf and Dumb in Milan for one of her Religious, who was to obtain the specialist qualification.

Most esteemed Marchioness,

  1. I received your most esteemed letter; I cannot tell you how pleased I was to hear how you have taken up what I asked of you;2 I assure you that I am and always will be most grateful, and I am certain God will reward you for what you are doing for him.

  2. Good Marchioness, here I am again imploring your kindness to bring this work to completion. I must tell you that the Director of the Royal Institute in Milan3 replied that I myself must petition the Ministry in order to obtain a free place, and he added that the Ministry has three such places at its disposal.

  3. I therefore beg you to obtain one of these places, together with approval to sit the examination privately. Only you can do me so great a service, and I am sure you will not refuse me your help in this work of charity; I know your kindness and charity too well to doubt it.

  4. Trusting to obtain through you what I have asked, I thank you in advance, begging you to accept my most affectionate regards, and believe me your

most humble Sr. Anna Rosa Gattorno

P.S. I carried out your errand with Father Tornatore, who replied that he had not received any of your letters.

From its content it appears to be addressed to the same person as Letter 40, the Marchioness Fanny Trivulzio.

2 Cf. Letter 40.

3 Fr. Eliseo Ghislandi.

She asks her to pray that a community may be opened at Cerro. Spiritual confidences.

A.M.F. My Superior,

  1. Two lines to ask for your news, which I want to hope will be good. Write to me in your own hand, to set my mind at rest.

  2. Listen, my dear: if things go well and I do not have to go to Milan for the Immaculate Conception, I will come to Cento.1 Then we will agree that you call me urgently, and I will come and stay with you for a few days.

  3. But God grant that we may rather have to go to Cerro.2 Pray that Saint Anne, our Mother, will grant this grace, which we need so much.

  4. Dear little daughter, if you knew how serious my troubles are, you would surely pity me, knowing how great is the love you bear this poor Mother of yours, who does not deserve it. A love which, I believe, certainly never departs from the Heart of Jesus, our only good and treasure. Isn't that so?3 My dear Francesca, if you could see this poor Mother of yours, how well she knows how to find you in that Heart! For when she says to Jesus, I entrust my Superior Francesca to you, where am I to put you to rest, if not in the cleft of his Side?4 There alone is found that dear balm that inebriates us.5

  5. I must close, for I feel unwell. I left one thing behind: the image of my Jesus on the bed at Cento. Keep it for me, and I will take it when I come back.

Goodbye; I can do no more, as you will see from the handwriting.

Goodbye; I am your most loving Mother Rosa

1 She went to Milan not only to visit her daughter Carlotta. She was still negotiating with Fr. Eliseo Ghislandi over the institution for deaf-mute girls. Cf. Letter 39.

2 She longed for the work to begin as soon as possible. She felt it was fully in harmony with the charism and an urgent need of so many poor deaf-mute girls, at risk or «already fallen».

3 A love whose source is in the Heart of Jesus; an entirely pure love, without any shadow of selfishness.

4 She tastes that love in the Heart of Jesus, and to Jesus she «entrusts», hands over, her Francesca.

5 «Dear balm that inebriates us»: a recurring expression in other letters to her daughters. In simple words it expresses the experience of union with God, which produces positive effects in the soul: exultation, invigorating strength, joy. (Cf Song 1 2*2,4'2, 11-13).

She offers to receive and suitably educate, in the house she has opened for orphan girls, all the girls [the Mayor] may wish to send.

Most Illustrious Mayor,

  1. The undersigned, having been informed that there are in this city a good many girls left orphans by the cholera that has afflicted us this year, and knowing that many of them are abandoned, without means of support or shelter, feels it her duty to turn to Your Most Illustrious Lordship and, after the most careful reflection, to place at the disposal of these poor girls the refuge for abandoned girls which the writer has opened in a house of hers at no. 49 Stradone Farnese.2

  2. Your Lordship may therefore arrange for all such girls3 as you consider deserving, being in the conditions described above, to be sent here; and the undersigned assures Your Lordship from now on that these girls will receive, besides free maintenance, the education proper to their station, and she trusts that one day they will be good mothers and good citizens.

  3. As this is a newly founded hospice and not yet provided with the necessary bedding, the undersigned would ask Your Lordship to place at the disposal of the girls admitted the number of beds you think fit, together with a small grant for their uniforms.

[.…Rosa Gattorno]

1 In the letter, of which the draft survives (Arch St FSA, A. 3. 37, Mmv 11),

the date is omitted; it is, however, recorded in the City Council's resolution in reply.

2 Cf. Letter 34.

3 In the first emergency she had had to make do with receiving only a few girls; now, with the facilities ready, she opens her arms to «all», without counting.

She asks to be told when the sisters are to go to the new work.

Very Reverend Parish Priest,

1. I beg Your Reverence to let me know whether it will still be long before I can come to you at Cerro with my Nuns. I should like to know, so as to be able to arrange the number of Religious that Your Reverence knows of. Please favour me with a prompt reply.

I hope you will always keep me among those you pray for, and with distinguished greetings I sign myself with the highest esteem and respect

Your Reverence's

most humble Sr. Anna Maria Rosa Gattorno

  1. I did not have the good fortune to see you when I went to Cento to hear from Your Lordship whether the poor nurses were still to Your Lordship's satisfaction; but I learned this from that excellent and wise Marquis, the Manager.2

Dear Superior,

  1. Here I am, my dear, up and about, and I am answering at once your dear letter, which I received today.

  2. Dear Superior, I am very sorry to hear that your health is still poor, and it worries me. I am preparing a Sister to send you; she is cheerful and very capable, and will be able to please everyone.1

  3. So see to it that Francesca helps Nunciata2 in the laundry, for charity's sake, so that she does not get lost in the accounts. If you see that she is not so much to the liking of the doctor or the others, I shall soon have had a letter from the Manager, to whom I wrote in reply to one of his which, I assure you, alarmed me, for he wrote that they keep up a smouldering, malicious fire3 against you; so I wrote at once to the President and to the Manager, but I assure you I am more anxious than ever. For charity's sake, do not speak of this to anyone.4 Let us pray that our Mother Saint Anne herself will remedy it. My dear, it really seems like the devil.

  4. You see that travel is expensive, and here we have enormous expenses for these girls. Gently remind the Bursar of what I had told him about Bernardi's 200 francs:5 that I was giving 50 to the Hospital, and the rest, you see, would be useful to me now, without spending the little that both you and I have put aside.

  5. My Francesca, then, if you could manage to get this out of the nurses' pay, I would come at once and bring Daria6 with me, and this A. M. Giuseppa.7 I would stay there a week and then come back here to Piacenza with you, and Rosa too; so everything would be left

in order and you could rest for a while to recover, for I am very afraid for you and it grieves me greatly. See whether you can obtain this. It would be a great good.

  1. Dear Francesca, burn this letter at once, because one never knows.8 I add no more, for I hope we shall see each other in a few days. I am also writing two lines to the Sisters to urge them to be patient.

  2. Goodbye, my Francesca, and be of good heart, for this poor Mother of yours always prays for you and loves you in the Heart of Jesus as much as one can love a daughter. See how badly I write when I have been writing for a while. It always happens to me.9

Greet Signora Irene for me, a handshake for Graziella, my respects to the doctor and to the Manager.10

Believe me always your Mother, who keeps you in mind, engraved in her mind,

and I am your most loving Mother Rosa

She was overjoyed at the news of her recovery. Being kept away from her during her short illness was painful. She gives her news of her brother and of Caterina Rapallino.

Dear daughter,

  1. Your few lines were a great consolation to me, telling me that you are up and in perfect health.

  2. My dear Carlottina, how painful it was for me not to be able to be near you in those few days when you were in bed! I would gladly have done so, as I had already resolved, had I not been prevented by this dreadful season,2 which is so fatal to my health and keeps me constantly by the fire.3

  3. Gigino writes asking me to give you his love, and he will soon write to you too; he is very happy at school, but he does not have holidays as you do; so, my Carlottina, try to be good and keep well, and in your holidays we will go and see him.

Receive a hug and a kiss from your most loving Mother, and from Caterina, who did not take the veil and whom you made laugh when you wrote to us about it, a tender hug and many greetings.

I am your

most loving Mother Rosa

She had returned to the school in Milan a few months earlier.

Winter in Piacenza is very harsh.

di cui... fuoco: so that I have to keep the stove lit.

Rosa Gattorno with Carlotta and Alessandro (c. 1864).

She asks for a donation for the third house about to be opened.

Most Reverend Eminence,

  1. Trusting in your kindness and charity, I venture to turn to Your Most Reverend Eminence to beg you to extend your beneficent hand to the third house,1 which is shortly to be opened but cannot be, since I lack 5,000 francs; I hope, however, to obtain them from the benefactors who gave me proof of their charity in the help they gave me in setting up this first house, foremost among whom is Your Eminence, of whom the furnishings of the chapel constantly remind us.

  2. I am sure you will not abandon this third house, which is in greater need than the others, since it is being established in a town without Religious,2 and souls there are therefore in extreme need of it.

  3. I hope to have the honour of a reply from you; be assured that letters reach me very well and none is ever lost. I leave this letter of mine in the hands of Jesus: may he carry it to Your Eminence and give strength to these poor words of mine, to obtain for his Work all that this donkey is asking.

Please accept a thousand good wishes for the coming holy feasts of Christmas and a happy new year, and believe me Your Eminence's

most humble Sr. Anna Maria Rosa Gattorno

1 The third house. This is presumably the institute for the education of young deaf-mute women at Cerro Maggiore (Milan). That foundation did not take place, however, nor did the one in Milan. Cf. Letter 63.

The third house was opened at Sampierdarena, but the following year, on 14 November 1868.

2 A second draft reads religion. Cf. Arch St FSA.

She replies to her letter. As regards the Hospital, she thinks those responsible for the administration should handle it. Christmas wishes and greetings.

Most esteemed Madam,

  1. I have received your very dear letter and was delighted to see from it that you are in good health, as is all your little family.

  2. As to what you tell me about the Hospital, I would still be of the opinion that everything should be left in the hands of the Bursar and the President: let them see to the good of the Hospital.3

  3. I take this opportunity to send both you and Signor Facchini, for these Christmas feasts, every good wish for a happy and prosperous season. Please accept a little Genoese sweet bread, which I will send on Christmas Eve.

Give dear Graziella4 a kiss from me, my warm greetings to your Husband, and believe me your

most humble Sr. Anna Maria Rosa Gattorno

1 Wife of the head physician of the hospital at Cento, Dr Didaco Facchini.

2 This letter is undated. But since it replies to the lady's letter of 17 December, it can be assigned to a day or so later.

3 During a visit to Cento the Mother had told her of a plan to take over entirely the service of the two wards, with the help of two male nurses for certain tasks. She had told her husband, who was in favour and wanted to propose it as his own.

4 The lady's daughter.

She returns his good wishes and hopes to meet him and receive his blessing in person.

Very Reverend Canon,

  1. How welcome were your letter and the good wishes you send this poor House! May God return them to you by blessing the works Your Reverence has undertaken with such zeal and labour.

  2. As I am shortly to pass through Genoa, I hope to have the happiness of kissing your hand and receiving your blessing.

Please accept my wishes for happiness and prosperity for the coming holy feasts, together with a good beginning [of the year].

Accept the sentiments of esteem and respect with which I have the honour to sign myself Your Reverence's

humble Sr. Anna Rosa Gattorno

1 As this is a draft, the addressee's name is missing, perhaps omitted because he was well known. He is thought to be Canon Felice Botta, who corresponded with Mother Rosa. Arch. St FSA, G 7.

She apologises for her delay in thanking him for a favour to people she had recommended. She asks for prayers.

Very Reverend Don Bosco,

  1. How many apologies I owe Your Reverence for my delay in fulfilling so great a duty! But since the cause was my illness, which was followed by a worse one that kept me seriously ill in bed, now that I am, I would say, barely recovered, I make an effort to dictate as best I can these few ill-connected lines, which would like to express so much, with the most heartfelt gratitude for the great favour of charity and solicitude you showed to those I recommended to you.

  2. Good Priest, I assure you that the good wishes and greetings you sent me were extremely welcome, but my wish would be far more fully satisfied if I could have two lines from you sending me your Blessing.

Confident that my wish will be granted, I sign myself Your Reverence's

most humble Sr. Anna M. R. G.

3. P.S. Please remember me before the Lord, for I am in extreme need, both spiritual and temporal; of the latter I can only tell you, to give you an idea of our need, that we are 70 people, all kept from day to day by providence.

1 In view of the detail in the P.S., «we are 70 people», the letter is presumed to have been written in November–December 1867.

She assures her of daily prayer for her health and her brother's. She has received the donation through Fr. Donadio.

Most Illustrious Marchioness,

  1. I received your most esteemed letter, in which I read that your health has improved a little. Be assured that we never cease to pray daily for Your Ladyship, and I hope you will recover your good health, as will your Most Reverend brother.2

  2. I take the occasion of the coming new year to wish you and all your excellent family every happiness and prosperity.

  3. I received Donadio's letter;3 I thank you infinitely for the offering you sent me. May God repay it a hundredfold. Please accept my greetings, together with those of Father Tornatore, who wishes you every happiness, and believe me your

most humble Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

1 She had met her in Rome in January 1866, as appears from the letter of Mgr Giambattista Fratejacci of 8 March 1866, which passes on greetings from her and her brother Cardinal Consolini. The Archive holds 9 letters from the Marchioness Brigida Ferrari to Mother Rosa.

2 Cardinal Domenico Consolini.

3 Fr. Agostino Donadio, a mutual friend.

Most noble Countess,

  1. I have had the high honour of being authorised, with the approval of His Holiness the Supreme Pontiff, to found an Institute whose purpose is the home nursing of the sick poor and the sheltering of girls at risk.

  2. Meanwhile, since this is a pious and philanthropic institution always protected and assisted by Your Ladyship's piety and munificence, I take courage to address this letter to you, since such an institution must be supported by the offerings of eminent and wealthy persons, to ask you to contribute whatever help Your Ladyship thinks best.

Hoping to obtain much and to have the honour of a reply from Your Ladyship, I declare myself with the most perfect consideration

Your Ladyship's

most devoted, most obliged Servant

Sr. Anna Maria Rosa Gattorno

1 This letter (preserved as a draft copy) does not bear the addressee's name, and it is impossible to guess which of the various titled benefactresses she was. The letter, clear and well argued, is of considerable historical value. To obtain what God's Work needed, the Foundress knew how to find the right tone, the apt expressions and the right approach. And she held out her hand on behalf of others, in person or in writing.

2 Given the context, the date can be attributed to the Institute's first years, presumably 1867, because the phrase «always protected and assisted» suggests a certain continuity over time.

She could not write to him immediately after her return because of her health. She urges him to do himself credit and to respect and obey his teachers. It will comfort her to hear that he is good, studious and obedient.

My dear son,

  1. After much suffering I reached Piacenza; I could not send you two lines at once because I was still unwell. Now I am better, and I take the opportunity at once to spend a little time with you.

  2. I hope, my dear Gigino, that by now you have found contentment at school, cared for by your good superiors,1 who will fill the gap left by my departure. So try, dear Gigino,2 to do yourself credit and to see your teachers in the person of the Lord; and so3 love them with all respect and reverence and obey them, for this, dear Gigino, is all you can do to give your poor Mother comfort and joy amid, as you know, so many other irreparable sorrows.

  3. My only comfort will be to hear that you are good, studious and obedient, and I do not want to doubt it. Write to me often; I am still waiting for letters from you. Try to be cheerful, and believe me always

your most loving Mother Rosa

1 Alessandro had already had a bad experience at a school in Genoa. For a few months he had been at the school in Savona run by the Priests of the Mission, Fr. Tornatore's confreres.

2 The family pet name.

3 Therefore.

She regrets having little good news to give her about her sister, who has been with the Daughters of Saint Anne for a year. She has relapsed into her illness, so she cannot remain in the Institute. No care, medicine or attention has been spared. She must be withdrawn. The small sum she brought cannot be returned, because the Institute has spent much more on her for medicine and clothing.

  1. I am very sorry to have to give this description, but the content of your letter obliges me to do so.

  2. Please reply at once, so that I may know what to do and take the measures her present state of health requires.

Believe me yours

most humbly, Rosa Gattorno

1 Sister of the postulant Laura Bonelli, who entered the Institute on 1 April 1867, recommended by Signora Paola Airenta of Genoa, a friend of Mother Rosa.

2 La di cui...: whom I have kept with me, since her mental illness has become acute during this period.

3 Necessary.

She has received her letter and is grateful for her kindness. She prays, and will go on praying, for her, unworthy though she is.

Dear Marchioness,

  1. How welcome was your most esteemed letter of the 3rd of this month, which I would have answered at once, as was my duty, to thank you for so much kindness, but my health prevented me.

  2. Good Marchioness, you ask me to pray; and how could one forget so great a benefactress? Every day I never cease to raise prayers for you to the Most High, that he may be pleased to grant all your wishes; but since, beloved in Jesus, these prayers have no strength and are of little worth, coming from a wretched sinner who can do nothing and knows nothing, they are not heard.

I gave your greetings to the Father. Believe me, in the Heart of Jesus,

your most obliged friend Rosa Gattorno

1 In all probability the Marchioness Brigida Ferrari. Cf. Letter 58.

Their plan seems impossible to carry out. God's will be done; let them wait in prayer for what they desire to be fulfilled.

Very Reverend Parish Priest,

  1. I received your most esteemed letter.2 Let us adore the will of the Lord, our only treasure, and bless his most divine hand, which deigns to make us [suffer] but never leaves ours abandoned.3

  2. Very Reverend Parish Priest, let us always trust in the Lord's goodness and mercy, and we shall find that for your dear Parish all is not over, but that, as from a very dark night, the dawn of a most happy morning will break. Let us pray, let us pray that everything can be accomplished.4

Write to me often; it will please me. Accept the sentiments of my most heartfelt esteem and respect, and believe me Your Reverence's

most humble Sr. Anna Maria Rosa Gattorno

1 Cf. Letter 49.

1 This letter has not survived. Its content can be inferred from this reply. Mother Rosa already knew of the obstacles, having been told by Fr. Ghislandi on 27.12.1867: «the Parish Priest of Cerro, at the express wish of the Archbishop, is abandoning further steps».

3 Let us adore the will of the Lord, which is our only treasure, and bless his most divine hand, which deigns to make us suffer but does not leave our hands tied, unable to do good.

She gives her news of her health.

A.M.F.

My dear little daughter,

  1. No sooner up than overwhelmed with work — you can imagine: I redid all the house's books1 and so many things — and always in poor health; today, and indeed since yesterday, I am swollen.

  2. Dear Caterina, this donkey2 is bending under the heavy load the Lord is pleased to put on its back.

Goodbye, my dear; when shall I embrace you?3 The Lord's will be done.

I am yours for ever, your most loving Mother Rosa

1 She bound and covered the books used in the community.

2 Her own body is seen through the lens of the spirituality of the time. Saint Francis of Assisi, with natural gentleness and evangelical spirit, called it brother ass.

3 The young woman was certainly at home with her family.

The two deaf-mute girls are ready to leave for Milan; she asks him to have them escorted.

Very Reverend Director,

  1. I received your most esteemed letter. 1. I reply to what Your Reverence asks me about the deaf-mute girls. They are ready to come,1 and I gladly bless the Lord for the providence that has favoured these two dear creatures; and may the Lord bless you too, very reverend Sir, for the great care you take on behalf of this unfortunate humanity.2

  2. I am very sorry not to be able to escort them myself because of my illness, which obliges me, as you see, to dictate, since I am not yet able to write to you in my own hand. It would be very kind of Your Reverence to send for them, as I have no one who can accompany them.

  3. Thank you for the good news you give me of Carlotta; at the same time I reply to your last esteemed letter about what you ask concerning her. My wish is this: I think that, for the girl's good, you should not hand her over to anyone, but only let her be seen when she has visitors. Tell everyone that, as she is now older,3 her mother does not want her to leave the side of her teachers, with whom she is so happy.

Accept the sentiments of esteem and respect with which I have the honour to sign myself Your Reverence's

Sr. Anna Maria Rosa Gattorno

4. P.S. So as not to show partiality, I am obliged to forgo the 148

undeserved kindnesses and favours Signora Radice4 shows my Carlottina; as soon as I come to Milan it will be my duty to go and thank her. I ask Your Reverence to let Signora Radice read these two lines, and meanwhile to give her my warmest greetings and ask her always to believe me her

most humble, most obliged Servant

She gives a good report of two young deaf-mute women who had stayed at the Mother House.

Most Illustrious Madam,

  1. I hasten to reply to your most esteemed letter, which I had the pleasure of receiving. I am glad to give you the information you ask about the two dear little angels you have with you, Emilia Ravasi and Teresa Villa.2 These two creatures are exceedingly good and sensible and have all the virtues that can satisfy their benefactresses.

  2. I thank you, dear Madam, for your kind invitation, and reserve for a personal meeting my good wishes for the work you have begun.

Accept the sentiments of esteem and respect of one who has the honour to call herself your

most humble Sr. Anna Maria Rosa Gattorno

1 A member of the religious Congregation of the «Pious Ladies of Nazareth», to whom the Institute for Deaf-Mute Girls had recently been entrusted after the failure of the negotiations with Mother Rosa.

2 Cf. Letter 65.

Teaching on the life of prayer. She asks for news.

A.M.F.

Dear Caterina,

  1. For many days now I have been in perfect health; on the day you left, my dear, I was very ill in the morning and then it all passed; so now I am well, except for my eyes and hands, which still tremble.

  2. Dear Caterina, our separation only increases my affection for you, and I keep saying: what will become of my little daughter? Every moment, and then to our holy Mother: for charity's sake, my Saint Anne, keep for me what you have given me.2

  3. Dear creature, love Jesus and keep him always pressed to your heart; during the day bow your head a little towards your heart and say to Jesus, who is hidden within: my love, I want to be all yours and you all mine, dear Jesus. Another time: my beloved, what are you doing in here alone in so small a dwelling? Ah! speak to me and calm my doubts, confirm me in your love, Jesus my Redeemer, give me your love.3

  4. If I were not afraid this letter might be lost, I would write you many things, but with this fear I will stop. Patience! Jesus will speak for me.

  5. I am in the greatest anxiety, though I do not know what to think: so many days without letters, and I do not even know whether you received mine. Write to me, but above all, come, dear Caterina. That is enough for now.

Goodbye; greet Sr. A. Francesca4 for me, and I am all yours, your poor

but most loving Mother, Sr. Anna Maria Rosa

1 Through an evident slip, Mother Rosa dated this letter, like the one written to Francesca the next day (cf. Letter 69), in February (8.2.1868) instead of 8.3... This is clear from the postmark, plainly visible on the back together with the address: To Signora Caterina Rapallino/ at the house of Signora Maria Cavanna/ ai Negri di Barmajano/ Bettola/. Cf. Letter 68, n. 1.

2 Convinced of the young woman's religious vocation, the Mother tends her dear little plant with attentive delicacy.

3 Suggestions on the life of prayer suited to her daughter's spiritual journey; she had now decided to follow Jesus closely among the Daughters of Saint Anne, yet she was still questioning herself and found obstacles in her parents' refusal of consent. Cf. Rapallino's letter to M. Rosa of 1867.

4 Sr. A. Francesca Camisa.

Distressed by Caterina's illness and her Daughters' absence, she asks for news.

A.M.F.

My dear little Daughters,

  1. What grief I felt on reading Francesca's letter! Even now I find no rest; I keep saying: my God! and then to the Superior: if only I knew whether my Caterina is still in bed!2 What will become of my dear little daughters? My Saint Anne, our Mother, bring them back to me at once, for their absence is too painful for me; the anxious thought is devouring me. Little daughters, hurry, come quickly to the bosom of one who is waiting for you and longs to embrace you affectionately.

  2. My dears, my health has recovered; for two days I have been at the loom, working; only I find writing very hard, and this is the first thing I have written since you left. It seems a century.

  3. Write to me at once with news of Caterina, for I have decided to come and fetch you. Maria is coming on Friday.3 Come, and write to me, and I will come at once; do not leave me in anxiety.

  4. Ah, my little daughters, it is better to stay under mamma's skirts than to travel; poor things, you did it out of obedience, and obedience saved you.4 God bless you and grant that you may always be ready to give your life for this obedience, so as to have heaven for ever.

  5. Pray, as we are praying; tomorrow morning there will be benediction at the holy Mother's altar in thanksgiving,5 that she may soon get my Caterina back on her feet.

I am for ever your most loving Mother, Sr. Anna Rosa

1 At the beginning of March Sr. A. Francesca Camisa and Caterina Rapallino — perhaps a third as well, though she is never mentioned — had gone to Bettola (Piacenza) to sell shawls made by the Sisters (cf. Letter 69, 7) and to buy provisions cheaply for the Mother House.

2 In a letter of 3 March Francesca had described the adventurous and disastrous journey. While crossing the swollen river Oglio the horse had balked, so that the coachman had to carry the sisters on his shoulders and they reached the other bank soaked. Both the fright and the unexpected bath had affected them, so that «Nina (Caterina) was in bed with a fever».

3 Maria Cavanna, the lady who was putting them up.

4 A note of spiritual formation is not lacking. The obedience asked in the Family of the holy Mother of Mary Immaculate is a goal of high perfection of love in following Jesus: to give one's life in order to have heaven for ever.

5 Sr. A. Francesca had asked for prayers of thanksgiving to Saint Anne for their escape from danger on the journey.

She asks for news and wants them to return as soon as possible.

A.M.F.

My dear Francesca, my daughter,

  1. All you have done is very good; indeed, always do the same, for you, my dear, know the needs of this house.1

  2. I hope you feel better now; but, my Francesca, what grief your letter today caused me! I would have flown into your arms, but an obedience held me back.2

  3. Patience; I am sending the gardener to get news of you and bring you what you ask for in your letter.3

  4. My dear, take care of yourself; for charity's sake, come back quickly into my arms, my dears, for I am impatient to have you near me, all because I know you are in such a bad way.

  5. By now you will also have Maria4 with you, who will cook for you and help you. If you think fit to send anything by the gardener, let me know by letter, not by word of mouth through the gardener, how you are and how business stands.5

  6. Mind, we have no more firewood; tell Maria, and send me money to pay the carter and the carriage of the goods, for it will come to a tidy sum.6

  7. Tell Maria too to send seed potatoes; as for the money, speak to Maria, not to Sister Gabriella, as I think this best for many reasons. If you have sold the shawls, come, come quickly.

Goodbye; I am your most loving

Mother Rosa

2 The news of Caterina's and Francesca's health was not at all good. Cf. Letter 70, 2.

3 The Mother House gardener would take what Caterina wanted: the blessed oil (cf. Letter 29, n. 1) and the «cigarettes» for asthma.

She confides her distress at Caterina's poor health.

A.M.F.

My dear, beloved little daughter Caterina,

  1. Believe me, this poor Mother of yours shares your suffering and perhaps feels the pain more than you do;2 your absence and the hardships that have befallen you confirm me in deciding that this will be the last time that, as far as I am concerned, you set foot outside without your poor Mother's feet going first.3

  2. My Caterina, as soon as I received Francesca's letter I wanted to fly to you, and I immediately sent the Superior to the Father for permission, but he, fearing for my health, said no. Patience!

  3. Courage, my dear; I hope that by now you are a little better, but to set my mind at rest I am sending you the gardener, because, from what I see, letters are getting lost; I have already written to you twice, and I read in yours that you have received none.

  4. Dear Caterina, our good Jesus wants to test us in every way, but believe me, these trials serve to set the rudder of the boat properly, so that it can sail on without coming to grief.4 Yes, my dear, let us run swiftly along the road of holiness.

  5. My health is excellent; since you left I do not seem the same person: I work, write, embroider, go out5 on foot. I am waiting impatiently for you so that we can go to Milan.

  6. I feel as though I had no arms;6 I go into your room and it saddens me always to see that bed made in the same way. Tomorrow, dear Caterina, my Communion will be all for you, offering it to our dear Mother Saint Anne, because Tuesday is dedicated to her, and this dear Mother will surely heal you. My Angel, Fr. Bernardo, will

be a good doctor to you;7 meanwhile I am sending you the cigars,8 though I know that by now you will not need them any more, and the oil too.9

7. Come soon, and send me good news, which I am impatiently awaiting; I have many things to tell you, but I will tell you them all in person.

Goodbye, my dear; receive a thousand blessings from one who loves you dearly, who calls herself your poor but ever most loving

Mother Rosa

2 Motherly love becomes empathy.

4 She teaches her the value of suffering, which makes us strong and steady and helps us grow. To set the rudder properly: to learn to steer our boat so that it can reach harbour without disaster.

5 I go out on foot.

6 Caterina helped her as secretary in writing her letters.

7 Father Bernardo Maria Clausi. Cf. Index III.

9 Cf. Letter 29, 1.

Most esteemed Madam,

  1. It is a long time, dear Marchioness, since I had news of you; I would have liked to ask you the reason sooner, but as I could not do so in my own hand, I refrained.

  2. Now I really want to venture to put together two ill-connected lines to tell you how much this most wretched creature always feels she owes you in thanks and gratitude for all you have done, of which I shall keep an eternal memory.2

  3. I hope your health is good; mine no longer exists, but by the mercy of dear, good Jesus I have been up for more than a month now and can attend to everything.

  4. Keep me always in your memory, and this poor Community too, which always prays for you that the Lord may fulfil your wishes.

  5. I sent His Eminence Consolini a copy of the Constitutions with a couple of lines, which I hope he received.

If it is not too much trouble, commend me to your prayers, as Your Ladyship does not forget this

most humble Sr. Anna Maria Rosa Gattorno

Very Reverend Canon,

  1. Today I was extremely sorry to be told that Your Reverence had taken the trouble to call on me, as I had many things to say; so I was very upset that they did not call me so that I could speak with you.

  2. So I will now tell you in writing what I would have liked to say in person: I thank you with all my heart for the offer Your Reverence kindly made me; I greatly appreciated it and shall remember it. I would gladly accept it, were it not for the sole reason that everything is done by our Confessor, as we have no services.2
